families.s: HSE respiratory-protective-equipment programme, selection, use and maintenance guidance
families.t: risk-based RPE selection, adequacy, suitability, training, supervision, pre-use checks, maintenance, records, storage and disposal
f: RPE should be selected for the wearer, the task and the environment.
RPE should be used only after other reasonably practicable control measures have been taken and its use justified by risk assessment.
The selected RPE must fit, be suitable for the task and wearer, and work with other protective equipment.
Wearers must be trained and supervised in correct use.
Each device must be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions and stored correctly.
An effective RPE programme includes correct selection, training, supervision, pre-use checks, maintenance, required records, storage and disposal.
Selection, maintenance and testing records should be retained where required.
Incorrect selection or misuse can invalidate protection and has contributed to serious accidents and fatalities.
families.g: RPE suitability depends on contaminant, concentration, oxygen level, task, wearer, facepiece, protection factor, other PPE, fit, maintenance, storage and the actual work environment.

families.t: individual facepiece fit, competent testing, model and size control, facial hair, fit checks and test-equipment hygiene
f: Tight-fitting RPE cannot protect the wearer if it leaks, and poor fit is a major cause of leakage.
Fit testing should be carried out during initial selection so users can choose from adequate models.
Each wearer should be fit tested for each type of tight-fitting facepiece they use.
The successful make, model, type and size should be made available for the wearer's use.
Fit testing should be carried out by a person who is appropriately trained, qualified and experienced.
Facial hair or other features in the sealing area can prevent an effective face seal.
Fit testing does not replace a wearer fit check each time the facepiece is put on.
Reusable fit-test filters and equipment handled between tests should be cleaned or disinfected appropriately.
families.g: A passed fit test applies to the tested wearer and exact facepiece configuration; changes in model, size, facial features, dental work, weight or other PPE can require reassessment.

families.s: HSE personal-protective-equipment selection, compatibility, provision and maintenance guidance
families.t: risk assessment, free provision, worker involvement, certification, fit, compatibility, cleaning, storage, defect reporting and review
f: Employers must provide PPE free of charge where a risk assessment shows it is needed.
PPE is used for residual risks after engineering controls and safe systems of work have been applied.
Selection should consider who is exposed, the hazard, exposure duration and exposure amount.
Workers should be involved in selection because this improves understanding and use.
PPE should suit the user and account for size, fit, compatibility, weight and physical characteristics.
PPE supplied for workplace use should meet the relevant product-safety requirements and carry applicable conformity marking.
Reusable PPE must be cleaned, maintained and stored in suitable clean and dry conditions.
Workers must use PPE properly and report loss, damage or obvious defects, while employers monitor use and review changes.
families.g: PPE effectiveness depends on the residual hazard, correct type and rating, fit, compatibility, user needs, training, wear time, cleaning, replacement, storage and supervision.

families.s: HSE upper-limb-disorder and repetitive-task assessment guidance
families.t: repetition, force, posture, duration, recovery, psychosocial factors, ART assessment, task redesign and early reporting
f: Upper limb disorders can affect the neck, shoulders, arms, wrists, hands and fingers.
Prolonged repetitive work, forceful actions and awkward or static postures are common risk factors.
The ART tool helps assess common risk factors in repetitive upper-limb tasks.
Risk reduction can include breaking up prolonged repetitive work with regular changes of activity.
Work height, angle and position should be adjusted where possible to suit the person performing the task.
Equipment should be suitable for the task and should not place undue strain on the user.
Workers should report symptoms early so risks and controls can be reviewed.
Task duration, recovery time, work organisation, environment, psychosocial factors and individual differences should be considered.
families.g: ULD risk depends on repetition, force, posture, duration, recovery, tool design, vibration, temperature, work organisation, psychosocial factors and individual health.

families.s: HSE COSHH assessment and good-control-practice guidance
families.t: hazardous-substance identification, prevention, substitution, source control, enclosure, ventilation, procedures, training, maintenance and emergencies
f: COSHH requires employers to assess risks from substances hazardous to health.
Employers must prevent exposure or, where prevention is not reasonably practicable, adequately control it.
Controls can include total or partial enclosure, local exhaust ventilation, general ventilation, procedures and RPE.
Processes should be designed and operated to minimise emission, release and spread at source.
Assessments should include storage, handling, disposal and foreseeable accidents, incidents or emergencies.
Workers must receive suitable information, instruction and training about hazards and controls.
Control measures must be properly used, maintained, examined and tested as required.
Hazardous substances can include chemicals, products, fumes, dusts, vapours, mists, gases and biological agents.
families.g: COSHH control depends on substance hazards, quantity, form, route, task, frequency, process conditions, control reliability, maintenance, worker behaviour and emergency arrangements.

families.t: GB WELs, long- and short-term limits, exposure monitoring, ALARP control and use of current EH40 values
f: Workplace exposure limits are occupational exposure limits approved for use in Great Britain.
Current GB WELs are listed in EH40 Workplace exposure limits.
EH40 includes long-term and short-term exposure limits for listed substances.
WELs are only one part of COSHH control and do not replace prevention or adequate control.
Exposure to carcinogens, mutagens and asthmagens must be controlled to as low as is reasonably practicable.
Exposure monitoring may be needed to demonstrate that controls are adequate or a WEL is not exceeded.
The latest EH40 values supersede limits printed in older guidance sheets.
Compliance with a WEL does not by itself prove that all health risks are adequately controlled.
families.g: Interpretation of a WEL depends on substance identity, sampling fraction, averaging period, mixture effects, task pattern, monitoring method, uncertainty and the duty to minimise exposure.

families.s: HSE safety-data-sheet, GB CLP and UK REACH communication guidance
families.t: hazard classification, labels, pictograms, precautionary information, SDS supply, exposure scenarios and COSHH use
f: Safety data sheets are required by UK REACH for hazardous chemicals supplied for use at work.
An SDS is important for safe supply, handling and use but is not itself a workplace risk assessment.
SDS information helps employers carry out a COSHH assessment.
GB CLP governs classification, hazard labelling and packaging of chemicals placed on the Great Britain market.
Hazard labels can include pictograms, signal words, hazard statements and precautionary statements.
Suppliers should provide an up-to-date SDS where the legal supply criteria apply.
REACH exposure scenarios can communicate risk-management measures for identified uses.
Users should compare SDS and label information with actual workplace quantities, processes, exposure routes and controls.
families.g: SDS and label information describes supply hazards and recommended controls; it does not establish actual workplace exposure or replace a task-specific COSHH assessment.

families.s: HSE acetylene use, cylinder identification and emergency guidance
families.t: flammability, decomposition, training, equipment, flashback protection, cylinder colour, licensing, transport and heated-cylinder response
f: Acetylene is extremely flammable and can form an explosive atmosphere with air or oxygen.
Acetylene should be used only by trained people with suitable equipment.
Safe systems should include correct regulators, hoses, non-return devices and flashback protection where required.
Compressed acetylene cylinders must use the prescribed maroon colour identification.
Manufacturing, compressing or filling relevant acetylene cylinders requires a licence.
A heated acetylene cylinder can decompose internally and present a delayed explosion risk.
HSE advises immediate evacuation around a heated cylinder and contacting the fire and rescue service rather than moving or venting it.
Cylinder valves should be closed during vehicle transport to reduce leakage risk.
families.g: Acetylene risk depends on leakage, ventilation, cylinder condition and heating, pressure, equipment compatibility, ignition sources, flashback protection, handling, storage and emergency response.
